description: Limited household financial resources can affect access to food, housing, transportation, health care, and other conditions that shape health.
why_it_matters: Income affects much more than purchasing power. It can determine whether healthy options, stable housing, transportation, and preventive health care are realistically accessible.

description: Being without paid work while actively seeking employment. Job loss can affect income, food security, housing stability, insurance coverage, and stress.
why_it_matters: Employment can influence multiple health pathways at once. A disruption in work may affect income, insurance, food, housing, stress, and the ability to maintain health routines.

description: Difficulty maintaining safe, stable, and affordable housing. It can include unaffordable rent, frequent moves, eviction risk, or unstable living arrangements.
why_it_matters: Stable housing provides the foundation for sleep, food storage, medication routines, safety, and access to work and health care. Housing disruption can destabilize several of these at once.

description: Limited or uncertain access to enough food for an active, healthy life because household resources are insufficient.
why_it_matters: Food insecurity is not simply a nutrition problem. It can affect eating patterns, chronic stress, disease management, and the ability to prioritize preventive care.

description: Barriers such as cost, distance, transportation, or local availability can make nutritious food harder to obtain.
why_it_matters: People cannot consistently choose foods that are unavailable, unaffordable, or difficult to reach. The surrounding food environment therefore shapes individual choices.

description: Neighborhood conditions can make routine movement easier or harder through sidewalks, parks, safety, transportation, recreation access, and cost.
why_it_matters: Healthy behavior depends partly on opportunity. Communities can make activity safe and convenient—or require extra time, money, transportation, and effort.

description: Barriers to timely, affordable, and appropriate health care. Insurance is one factor, but provider supply, cost, transportation, language, and appointment access also matter.
why_it_matters: Preventing and managing chronic disease depends on more than medical knowledge. People need realistic access to screening, medications, clinicians, and ongoing follow-up.

description: Eating patterns that provide fewer nutritious foods or an unfavorable balance of nutrients. Diet quality is shaped by both individual choices and the surrounding food environment.
why_it_matters: Diet quality influences glucose regulation, cardiovascular health, body weight, and overall metabolic health, but it is also shaped by affordability and food access.

description: Insufficient routine physical activity relative to recommended levels. Activity is influenced by health, time, environment, resources, and opportunity.
why_it_matters: Physical activity affects glucose use, insulin sensitivity, cardiovascular health, strength, and body composition. Small differences can accumulate over time.

description: Higher levels of body fat can affect metabolic health and increase diabetes risk, although body weight is influenced by many biological, behavioral, and environmental factors.
why_it_matters: Excess adiposity can contribute to insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk. At the same time, weight is the result of many interacting biological and environmental factors.

description: A state in which cells respond less effectively to insulin. The body must produce more insulin to keep blood glucose within a normal range.
why_it_matters: Insulin resistance can develop long before Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed, creating an important opportunity for prevention before blood glucose reaches the diabetes range.

description: Blood glucose levels above the healthy range. Persistent elevation can reflect prediabetes or diabetes and may occur before noticeable symptoms.
why_it_matters: Elevated glucose can damage tissues over time even before a person feels unwell. Detecting abnormal glucose earlier can create opportunities for prevention and treatment.

description: A chronic metabolic disease in which blood glucose remains elevated because the body does not use insulin effectively and/or cannot produce enough insulin.
why_it_matters: Type 2 diabetes sits at the center of this network because its risk is shaped by upstream social, environmental, behavioral, and biological factors—and it can affect nearly every organ system.

description: Unusually strong or persistent thirst. In diabetes, high blood glucose can increase fluid loss through the kidneys and trigger thirst.
why_it_matters: Persistent thirst can be an early clue that glucose regulation is abnormal, especially when it occurs together with frequent urination.

description: Urinating more often than usual. When blood glucose is high, extra glucose in the urine can draw additional water with it.
why_it_matters: Frequent urination can signal elevated glucose but has many other possible causes, so persistent symptoms deserve proper evaluation.

description: Persistent tiredness or low energy. Diabetes can contribute to fatigue, but fatigue has many possible causes.
why_it_matters: Fatigue can strongly affect daily functioning, but because it has many possible causes it should be understood in the larger clinical picture rather than treated as diabetes-specific.

description: Reduced visual clarity or difficulty focusing. Blood glucose changes can temporarily alter vision, while diabetes can also damage the retina over time.
why_it_matters: Vision changes can be temporary, but diabetes can also cause progressive eye damage. Early evaluation can protect vision.

description: Nerve damage that can cause pain, tingling, numbness, weakness, or loss of sensation, especially in the feet.
why_it_matters: Neuropathy can reduce protective sensation, allowing injuries to occur without pain and increasing the risk of serious foot complications.

description: Damage that reduces the kidneys' ability to filter blood. Diabetes is a major cause of chronic kidney disease, which may progress without obvious early symptoms.
why_it_matters: Kidney damage often develops silently. Screening can identify disease before symptoms appear and allow treatment aimed at slowing progression.

description: Cardiovascular disease is an umbrella term for diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels. Coronary heart disease is one specific cardiovascular disease within this broader category.
why_it_matters: Diabetes and hypertension increase risk across several cardiovascular conditions. This broad node is retained to represent overall cardiovascular burden, while specific conditions such as coronary heart disease are shown separately when evidence and interventions are more specific.

description: A medical emergency caused by interrupted blood flow or bleeding in the brain. Diabetes is an established risk factor for stroke.
why_it_matters: Stroke can cause permanent disability or death. Many of its major risk factors—including diabetes and high blood pressure—can be identified and managed.

description: Diabetes can damage blood vessels in the retina and other structures of the eye, potentially threatening vision.
why_it_matters: Diabetic eye disease may progress without noticeable symptoms. Routine screening can identify damage while treatment can still help preserve vision.

description: Diabetes-related nerve damage and poor circulation can increase the risk of wounds, infection, ulcers, and other foot complications.
why_it_matters: Small foot injuries can become serious when sensation and circulation are impaired. Prevention and early treatment can reduce the risk of infection and amputation.

description: Regularly consuming more sodium than the body needs can raise blood pressure in many people. Most dietary sodium comes from processed, packaged, and restaurant foods rather than the salt shaker alone.
why_it_matters: Sodium intake is modifiable, but it is also shaped by the food environment. Reducing sodium can help lower blood pressure, especially for people who are more salt-sensitive.

description: Persistent psychological or social stress can affect the nervous system, hormones, sleep, health behaviors, and cardiovascular function. Its health effects vary substantially from person to person.
why_it_matters: Stress is not a simple one-way cause of hypertension, but repeated or persistent stress can affect blood pressure directly and can also influence sleep, activity, eating, alcohol use, and engagement with health care.

description: A chronic condition in which the pressure of blood against artery walls remains above a healthy range. High blood pressure often causes no warning signs or symptoms but can damage the heart, brain, kidneys, and blood vessels over time.
why_it_matters: Hypertension is common, often silent, and treatable. Identifying and controlling it can reduce the risk of stroke, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and other serious outcomes.

description: Outdoor air pollution, including particle pollution, ozone, traffic-related pollution, and wildfire smoke, can irritate the airways and trigger asthma symptoms or attacks in susceptible people.
why_it_matters: People cannot fully control the air around them. Community air quality, transportation, wildfire smoke, and industrial emissions can shape exposure and asthma risk independently of individual behavior.

description: Damp indoor spaces and water damage can support mold growth. Breathing mold spores can trigger asthma symptoms or attacks in people who are sensitive to mold.
why_it_matters: Moisture and mold are partly housing conditions. Fixing leaks, controlling humidity, and remediating mold can reduce exposure in ways that medication alone cannot.

description: Secondhand smoke is tobacco smoke breathed by people who are not smoking. It can irritate the airways and trigger asthma attacks.
why_it_matters: Avoiding tobacco smoke is an important part of asthma control, but exposure may depend on household, workplace, housing, and public-space conditions rather than only on the person with asthma.

description: Dust mites, cockroach and pest allergens, pet dander, and other indoor allergens can trigger asthma symptoms in susceptible people.
why_it_matters: Trigger exposure is shaped by housing quality, moisture, pests, ventilation, and a person’s specific sensitivities, so effective control is often tailored rather than one-size-fits-all.

description: A chronic lung disease in which the airways become inflamed and narrow, making it harder to breathe. Symptoms and triggers vary from person to person.
why_it_matters: Asthma connects clinical care with the environments where people live, learn, work, and breathe. Good control often requires both appropriate treatment and reduction of relevant triggers.

description: A whistling or squeaking sound during breathing, often most noticeable when breathing out.
why_it_matters: Wheezing is a common asthma symptom, but it can have other causes. Its pattern, severity, and relationship to other symptoms help guide evaluation.

description: A feeling of not getting enough air or having difficulty breathing.
why_it_matters: Breathing difficulty can occur during asthma symptoms or attacks and can become urgent when severe or rapidly worsening.

description: A sensation of pressure, squeezing, or tightness in the chest that can occur when asthma narrows the airways.
why_it_matters: Chest tightness is a recognized asthma symptom, but chest symptoms can also have other causes and should be interpreted in context.

description: Coughing can occur with asthma, often at night or early in the morning, and may worsen with certain triggers or respiratory infections.
why_it_matters: Cough is common and nonspecific. In asthma, its timing and relationship to wheezing, breathlessness, triggers, or infections can be informative.

description: A period when asthma symptoms become significantly worse, sometimes called an asthma attack. Severe attacks can require urgent or emergency treatment.
why_it_matters: Asthma attacks can often be reduced through an action plan, appropriate medication use, follow-up care, and reduction of relevant environmental triggers.

description: High blood cholesterol (hyperlipidemia) means cholesterol levels—especially LDL cholesterol—are high enough to increase cardiovascular risk. It is usually identified with a blood test and often causes no symptoms.
why_it_matters: High LDL cholesterol contributes to atherosclerotic plaque buildup and increases risk for coronary heart disease and stroke. Risk reflects a mix of genetics, health conditions, diet, physical activity, tobacco exposure, and other factors.

description: Coronary heart disease occurs when plaque builds up in the coronary arteries and reduces blood flow to the heart muscle.
why_it_matters: CHD is a major form of heart disease and can lead to angina, heart attack, heart failure, disability, and premature death.

description: COPD is a chronic lung disease that causes persistent airflow limitation. It includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis and can make breathing progressively more difficult.
why_it_matters: COPD can substantially limit daily activity and quality of life. Tobacco smoke is the leading cause, while occupational and environmental exposures also contribute.

description: Cancer is a large group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow and can invade or spread to other parts of the body. Different cancers have different causes, risk factors, symptoms, treatments, and outcomes.
why_it_matters: Cancer is not one single disease. Tobacco, alcohol, excess body weight, and physical inactivity are established risk factors for particular cancer types, so broad arrows in this network should be interpreted as risk relationships for certain cancers rather than every cancer.

description: Depression is a mood disorder that can cause persistent sadness or loss of interest along with changes in sleep, energy, concentration, appetite, and daily functioning.
why_it_matters: Depression is common and treatable. Genetic, biological, environmental, psychological, social, and chronic-illness factors can all contribute to risk, and depression can also interact with physical health conditions.

description: Use of combustible tobacco products, especially cigarette smoking, exposes the body to toxic chemicals that damage the lungs, blood vessels, and many organs.
why_it_matters: Smoking is a major preventable cause of COPD, heart disease, cancer, stroke, and other chronic illness.

description: Alcohol consumption at levels that increase health risk, including binge drinking and heavy drinking patterns.
why_it_matters: Higher alcohol exposure contributes to several cancers and can worsen blood pressure, liver disease, injury risk, and mental health.

description: Repeated inhalation of dusts, fumes, chemicals, or other respiratory hazards in the workplace.
why_it_matters: Long-term workplace respiratory exposures can contribute to COPD and other lung disease, especially when combined with smoking or poor air quality.

description: Limited social contact, support, or meaningful connection with other people.
why_it_matters: Social isolation can affect mental health, coping, access to support, and the ability to manage chronic illness.

description: Chest pain or discomfort caused when the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen-rich blood.
why_it_matters: Angina can be a warning sign of coronary artery disease and should be medically evaluated.

description: A heart attack occurs when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked long enough to damage heart muscle.
why_it_matters: Heart attack is a life-threatening complication of coronary artery disease and requires emergency treatment.

description: A COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation.
why_it_matters: Exacerbations can lead to urgent care, hospitalization, faster loss of lung function, and reduced quality of life.

description: Problems with sleep timing, duration, continuity, or quality.
why_it_matters: Sleep changes are common in depression and can worsen mood, energy, concentration, and physical health.

description: Reduced ability to focus, sustain attention, or make decisions.
why_it_matters: Difficulty concentrating is a common symptom of depression and can interfere with school, work, and daily functioning.
